title: The One With The Worst Best Man Ever

jokes.text: That was the 10th time I've peed here. / It's also the 10th time you've told us.
jokes.setup: Phoebe announces with apparent pride that she has peed for the 10th time
jokes.punchline: Rachel flatly notes it's also the 10th time Phoebe has told them, deflating the overshare
jokes.explanation: Solid opener — the straight-man deflation of an oversharing pregnant woman is well-timed and efficient. Rachel's retort is clean and characterful.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I have to pee again. That's the third time this hour!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Phoebe, you've announced that you have to pee three times this hour.

jokes.text: Sorry, it must be hard to hear. / It's easier having babies playing 'Bring in Da Funk' on your bladder!
jokes.setup: Someone sympathizes that it must be hard to keep announcing the bathroom trips
jokes.punchline: Phoebe one-ups the complaint with the absurd image of babies playing 'Bring in Da Funk' on her bladder
jokes.explanation: The specific cultural reference ('Bring in Da Funk' was a huge Broadway show at the time) combined with the visceral image of babies using her bladder as a percussion instrument is genuinely inventive. Very Phoebe — she escalates complaints into poetry. Earns its score.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: The baby's been kicking so much, it feels like there's a whole Broadway show going on in there.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That sounds uncomfortable.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: It is! It's like 'Stomp'.

jokes.text: I am so sick of being pregnant! My only happiness is from a cup of coffee — which is decaf because I'm pregnant!
jokes.setup: Phoebe declares her only happiness is coffee
jokes.punchline: The punchline immediately undercuts the comfort — it's decaf, rendering it essentially symbolic
jokes.explanation: The circular logic (the one joy is negated by the reason she needs joy) is tight and self-contained. Good economy, relatable pregnancy humor.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I can't have coffee because of the baby, I can't have sushi because of the baby, I can't have a nice soft cheese because of the baby. The only thing that makes me happy is eating, and I can't do that because of the baby!

jokes.text: You want a cookie? / Thank you so much!
jokes.setup: Monica offers a cookie as casual consolation to the complaining Phoebe
jokes.punchline: Phoebe accepts with overwhelming, emotionally disproportionate gratitude — implying pregnancy has reduced her to being pacified by cookies
jokes.explanation: The humor is in the gap between the smallness of the offer and the enormity of the gratitude. Very economical — four words total does the work. Slightly thin but effective.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Have you been having mood swings?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No! I haven't had mood swings!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Phoebe, you just had one.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No I didn't!

jokes.text: So, honey, how are those mood swings coming? / I haven't had any yet.
jokes.setup: Monica asks about mood swings, implying she's observed some; Phoebe has just been wildly emotional and complaining
jokes.punchline: Phoebe answers with complete sincerity that she hasn't had any yet — total lack of self-awareness is the joke
jokes.explanation: Classic dramatic irony — the audience and Monica both know Phoebe is exhibiting mood swings in real time. The deadpan delivery of the denial is excellent character comedy. Phoebe's obliviousness is a consistent trait, well deployed here.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh my God! Yes! Yes, I will marry you!

jokes.text: Here's the ring. / Yes, yes! A thousand times, yes!
jokes.setup: Ross hands Joey the engagement ring to hold as best man
jokes.punchline: Joey immediately treats it as a marriage proposal directed at him and dramatically accepts
jokes.explanation: Joey's self-centered interpretation of literally everything through his own lens is pitch-perfect character comedy. 'A thousand times, yes' is the right level of dramatic excess. Very Joey — he makes the moment about himself and it's endearing, not annoying.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I need to pick a best man.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh, wow. Okay, so you're not asking me?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, I haven't decided yet.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Could this BE any more awkward?

jokes.text: He got to do it at your first wedding. I figured you'd understand. I've known him longer. I don't have any brothers. I'll never be a best man.
jokes.setup: Ross explains to Joey why he already chose Chandler as best man
jokes.punchline: Joey's grievances escalate from logical ('he got to do it before') to absurdly melodramatic ('I'll never be a best man') in rapid succession
jokes.explanation: The escalation from reasonable complaint to existential lament is good Joey characterization. Lands solidly but doesn't transcend the formula.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Hey, I was thinking... when I get married, I want you to be my best man.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh man, that's great! Wait... you're gonna get married?

jokes.text: You can be the best man when I get married. / I'll never get to be a best man!
jokes.setup: Ross tries to console Joey by promising him the role at his own future wedding
jokes.punchline: Joey's self-awareness that he'll never get married, delivered as a punchline to his own melodrama
jokes.explanation: Joey's self-deprecating awareness about his romantic life is consistent characterization. The beat is well-timed and gets a solid laugh, though not a memorable one.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: This is impossible. This is like asking me to choose between Monica and Rachel.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Actually, no—I've done that. This is harder.

jokes.text: So you'll be my best man twice, and I won't be yours at all?
jokes.setup: Chandler has been listening to Ross promise Joey his future wedding's best man slot
jokes.punchline: Chandler points out the mathematical absurdity — he's been double-promised while being robbed once
jokes.explanation: Good Chandler moment — his logical accounting of emotional debts is characterful. Gets a mild laugh, competent sitcom writing.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, I'm honored. But I gotta say, I feel really bad for Chandler.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What? Why?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Because when this wedding's over, you're gonna be married. And I'm still gonna be Joey Tribbiani.

jokes.text: What about me? You said I could. / I'm not getting married! / It's a question for science-fiction writers.
jokes.setup: Ross says Chandler can be his best man; Chandler objects that Ross said the same to Joey
jokes.punchline: Ross says he's not getting married (again, implying he has no future marriages planned), then escalates to 'it's a question for science-fiction writers' — framing Chandler's hypothetical wedding as fantastical fiction
jokes.explanation: Chandler's romantic hopelessness being framed as a matter for 'science-fiction writers' is an inventive and sharp line. It's specific, funny, and rooted in Chandler's established character arc of fear of commitment. Good writing.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, the baby's kicking! Feel it!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That's amazing!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, but I think the other one's jealous. If they don't stop fighting in there, I'm gonna reach in and separate them!

jokes.text: I can't believe it's not me. How could it not be me? I'm not even... You know what? That's it. From now on, Joey will be my best man.
jokes.setup: Chandler spirals in self-pity about not being chosen as best man
jokes.punchline: Ross, fed up, impulsively switches his choice to Joey mid-argument — a reactive, petulant decision played as authority
jokes.explanation: Functional plot beat with mild comedy. Ross's petulant snap decision is in character, but the joke is thin. The humor is in the absurdity of the decision-making process, not any particular line.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Wait, what did she say?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I said, if you leave this apartment, I will rip your arms off and beat you with them!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: She's asking if you'll bring back some beer.

jokes.text: Shame about you, though. [Joey to Chandler after being named best man]
jokes.setup: Joey has just been awarded best man status at Chandler's expense
jokes.punchline: Joey delivers a brief, almost sympathetic 'shame about you, though' — casual and slightly callous about his friend's loss
jokes.explanation: Four-word joke that perfectly captures Joey's oblivious self-absorption with just enough warmth that it doesn't read as mean. The economy is exceptional — it does so much character work in so few words.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Why aren't we invited to the bachelor party?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: It's a bachelor party. You have to be a bachelor.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: We can be bachelors.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No, you have to be single guys. That's what a bachelor is.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: So if we pretend to be single guys—

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You can't pretend. You either are or you aren't. I don't make the rules.

jokes.text: It's not kicking me. It's kicking another baby.
jokes.setup: Someone notices Phoebe reacting to movement and suggests the baby kicking is a good thing
jokes.punchline: Phoebe clarifies that the baby is not kicking her but kicking another baby — sibling rivalry in utero
jokes.explanation: Genuinely surprising and delightfully dark. The concept of intrauterine sibling fighting is novel, the delivery is straight-faced, and the follow-up 'Don't make me come in there!' elevates it further. One of the sharper jokes in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: A baby shower? I'm not going to a baby shower. I don't even go to my own mother's birthday parties.

jokes.text: Don't make me come in there!
jokes.setup: Phoebe has just said her babies are fighting each other in the womb
jokes.punchline: She threatens them with the classic parental warning — as though she could actually intervene
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode's first act. The absurd logic is airtight: babies fighting → parental threat → 'Don't make me come in there' — the comedic concept of threatening to enter your own womb is surreal and perfectly Phoebe. It's immediately quotable, earns its laugh through pure comedic logic, and lands with great economy. Comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor — specific, unexpected, and highly repeatable.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I'm so excited! I'm having a party!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I just... I can't... *breaks into tears* Why am I crying?!

jokes.text: Get your ass back here, Tribbiani!
jokes.setup: Joey casually asks to borrow a bowl, mentions a party, and when told he should invite the girls, tries to bolt
jokes.punchline: Monica's authoritarian snap — using Joey's last name like a drill sergeant — is a funny contrast to her usual hostess warmth
jokes.explanation: Monica's controlling nature channeled into a cop-like bark. Decent character moment, gets a solid reaction.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: So I'm thinking about who to invite to my bachelor party, and I want to make sure I get all the right guys.

dialogue.speaker: Gunther
dialogue.line: I'll be there.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, what? I didn't even ask you.

dialogue.speaker: Gunther
dialogue.line: I heard you talking about it. I'm in.

jokes.text: Hormones. [Monica's one-word explanation for why she yelled at Joey]
jokes.setup: Monica just screamed at Joey to come back, then the girls turn to each other
jokes.punchline: Monica deflects her own controlling behavior by blaming Phoebe's pregnancy hormones — except she's not pregnant
jokes.explanation: One-word joke that does double duty: it's self-deprecating (Monica acknowledging her outburst) while also being a sly joke about pregnancy as a universal excuse. The word alone carries the laugh — excellent economy.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Paleontologists? Yeah, those dinosaur dudes are cool.

jokes.text: Are you bachelors? / Are you strippers? / Then you're not invited. / Then you're not invited to our party either.
jokes.setup: Joey says the girls aren't invited to Ross's bachelor party; Rachel and Monica push back
jokes.punchline: Joey's binary criteria (bachelor/stripper) for party eligibility; Monica and Rachel's retaliatory disinvitation from a party they haven't planned yet
jokes.explanation: The parallel structure (are you a bachelor / are you a stripper) is clean, and the counter-threat from Monica and Rachel builds nicely even before they know what their party is. Good situational comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay, so for the bachelor party, I'm thinking we get some beer, maybe some wine...

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Joey, that's it? That's your big plan?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What? I went to the store, I got a six-pack!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: A six-pack? Joey, there's gonna be like thirty guys there!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: So? We can always get more... I mean, I can always drink more.

jokes.text: What party? [Rachel's innocent response after retaliating with a party threat]
jokes.setup: Rachel has just threatened Joey with exclusion from 'our party' — except she made it up on the spot
jokes.punchline: She immediately breaks the bluff by asking what party she just threatened him with
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-word callback to Rachel's own bluff. The gap between the bravado and the confusion is the joke. Very economical — the 'What party?' lands because it immediately follows the threat.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh, so now you're too good for Atlantic City? What, you want to go somewhere fancy like the Hamptons or something?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: "Oh, I'm Ross Geller, I have a PhD in paleontology, I only celebrate life's milestones in places with Michelin stars."

jokes.text: Baby shower? That so doesn't sound like something I want to do.
jokes.setup: Monica announces that the party will be a baby shower for Phoebe
jokes.punchline: Rachel's immediate, transparent lack of enthusiasm — she's clearly going to do it anyway but can't pretend to be excited
jokes.explanation: Functional joke on Rachel's selfishness/honesty. Gets a mild laugh but it's predictable Rachel behavior without a clever twist.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, hey, hey! I didn't hire a stripper. This is my friend Candy. She's a dancer.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Joey!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What? You said no strippers. She's a dancer!

jokes.text: I can't believe I'm going to have a party. / That's so great. A party!
jokes.setup: Monica has just come up with the baby shower idea — ostensibly for Phoebe
jokes.punchline: Monica's excitement is transparently about throwing a party, not about honoring Phoebe — she's already forgetting the recipient
jokes.explanation: Monica's party obsession is a core character trait and this is a clean deployment of it — the barely-veiled joy that she gets to plan an event slightly overwhelms her concern for her friend.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: It's not a stripper rule, it's a 'we were on a break' rule.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh, right, right. I knew that. I just wasn't listening.

jokes.text: In terms of the invite list, I got you, me and Chandler. I'll invite Gunther because we're talking pretty loud.
jokes.setup: Joey is planning Ross's bachelor party; mentions inviting Gunther
jokes.punchline: The only reason Gunther is invited is that he overheard by accident — a tacit acknowledgment of Gunther's omnipresence at Central Perk
jokes.explanation: Smart meta-joke about Gunther's status as a peripheral but ever-present character — inviting him by accident of proximity rather than friendship is both funny and kind of sad. Gunther's 'I'll be there' response seals it perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, look at these little outfits! They're so tiny!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I know! It's like clothes for the Bee Gees!

jokes.text: I'll be there. [Gunther, responding to being accidentally invited]
jokes.setup: Joey mentions he'll invite Gunther because they're talking too loud
jokes.punchline: Gunther accepts immediately, confirming he was indeed eavesdropping and has no self-consciousness about it
jokes.explanation: Three words that perfectly encapsulate Gunther as a character: eager, slightly pathetic, completely unselfconscious. The beat works because it confirms the premise of the previous joke without explanation. Great Gunther characterization.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I know, but she's carrying our baby. The least we can do is make sure she's comfortable and well-dressed.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Monica, she's a surrogate. She's not a life-size doll.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I just want everything to be perfect for when the baby arrives.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: The baby arrives from inside of her, not from a shopping bag from Baby Gap.

jokes.text: I know it's your party, but I'd like to limit the number of museum geeks. Let's not invite any anthropologists. Just the dinosaur dudes.
jokes.setup: Joey is planning Ross's bachelor party invite list
jokes.punchline: Joey has a taxonomy of Ross's academic colleagues — 'museum geeks' split into anthropologists (bad) and 'dinosaur dudes' (acceptable) — implying he's thought about this before
jokes.explanation: Joey's condescending categorization of academics into acceptable/unacceptable subgroups is funny precisely because it has its own internal logic. 'Dinosaur dudes' is a great Joey phrase.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wait, so we're throwing a party for someone who's giving away their baby?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: When you say it like that, it sounds depressing.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm not trying to be depressing, I'm just saying — we're celebrating something really sad.

jokes.text: We'll need a six-pack of Zima.
jokes.setup: Joey is listing party supplies for what should be a lively bachelor party
jokes.punchline: He specifies Zima — a notoriously weak and unhip malt beverage, the antithesis of a wild party drink
jokes.explanation: A period-specific joke — Zima was famously uncool in the late 90s. The specificity of the brand does the comedic work. Somewhat dated now but landed at the time.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Okay, so I'm thinking we get you some really nice maternity clothes, and then some regular clothes for after the baby.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, that's so sweet! But, um, I'm gonna need clothes that can go from maternity to regular really quickly.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Why? How fast do you think you'll lose the weight?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No, because I'm gonna forget I'm pregnant and go back to my old lifestyle.

jokes.text: It won't be that difficult since this one won't be in the basement of a Pizza Hut. / I'm Ross, I'm Ross. I'm too good for the Hut.
jokes.setup: Chandler says the party won't be hard to top since the last one (at a previous wedding) was held in the basement of a Pizza Hut
jokes.punchline: Joey's mock impression of Ross's snobbery — 'I'm too good for the Hut' — delivered in a whiny voice
jokes.explanation: Two-beat joke: the reveal (Pizza Hut basement) is unexpected and funny on its own; Joey's impression adds character comedy. The specific mundanity of a Pizza Hut basement for a wedding is an inspired detail.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh wow, thank you so much! A diaper genie! You know, I've always wondered what I'd do if I had a regular genie and I wished for it to become a diaper genie.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: And look, a book on how to be a better mother. Wow. Because apparently I'm not doing a good job.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: And this... what is this? A breast pump? Oh great, so now I can be a cow in my spare time.

jokes.text: There will be strippers. He didn't say anything about no strippers. / He just said, 'No strippers.' / I chose not to hear that.
jokes.setup: Ross specifically asks for no strippers; Joey waits for Ross to leave before contradicting him
jokes.punchline: Joey's logic — 'I chose not to hear that' — is a perfectly absurd piece of motivated reasoning delivered without shame
jokes.explanation: One of the strongest jokes in the episode. 'I chose not to hear that' is a quotable piece of comic logic — it's not that Joey misheard or forgot, he actively exercised editorial control over his own perception. The three-beat structure (confident claim, correction, philosophical counter) is tight. Very Joey and genuinely funny. Approaches the 8.0 anchor benchmark.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What's your last name?

dialogue.speaker: Gunther
dialogue.line: Central?

jokes.text: They make these for little people! Little Village People.
jokes.setup: Rachel has bought baby gifts — miniature costumes that are Village People outfits for infants
jokes.punchline: The concept of dressing babies as the Village People is inherently absurd; 'Little Village People' is a perfect phrase
jokes.explanation: The visual gag works on two levels — the absurdity of the costumes themselves and Rachel's delight in them. The physical comedy of showing off tiny construction worker/cop/cowboy outfits is strong. Gets a bigger laugh from the sight gag than the line.

dialogue.speaker: Gunther
dialogue.line: Thanks, Ross. You know, I've always appreciated how you treat people around here.

dialogue.speaker: Gunther
dialogue.line: But I gotta be honest with you... I've been in love with Rachel for years.

jokes.text: Except she won't be the one who gets to dress them. / She won't get to keep the babies. / My God, we are throwing the most depressing baby shower!
jokes.setup: The girls are excited about baby shower gifts — cute baby clothes, etc.
jokes.punchline: The realization hits that Phoebe is a surrogate and won't be taking the babies home — all the cute 'mom' gifts are emotionally devastating
jokes.explanation: The pivot from cheerful gift excitement to sudden dark realization is well-constructed. The escalation from 'she can't dress them' to 'she won't keep them' to Monica's explosive verdict is a solid three-beat dark comedy moment.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: The best man position is open.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I also need a bride.

jokes.text: My God, we are throwing the most depressing baby shower!
jokes.setup: Monica and Rachel have just realized their shower gifts are inappropriate for Phoebe's situation.
jokes.punchline: Monica voices the audience's conclusion: this is objectively the saddest shower possible.
jokes.explanation: Good button line that names the joke directly. The self-aware acknowledgment of the situation's inherent tragedy-as-comedy is well-deployed.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, that's a great attitude, man. You know, most guys, they see the glass half empty. But you... you see the glass, and you just think about how nice it's gonna look in your wedding china.

jokes.text: Like regular coffee. Tequila! And those leather pants she's always wanted!
jokes.setup: To solve the depressing shower problem, the girls decide to give Phoebe gifts she can use after pregnancy — things she's been denied
jokes.punchline: The list escalates from sensible (coffee) to boozy (tequila) to absurdly specific (leather pants she's apparently always wanted) — implying they know Phoebe's deferred desires in great detail
jokes.explanation: The escalating list format is classic sitcom comedy. 'Leather pants she's always wanted' is the best item — the specificity suggests backstory we don't need explained. Good construction.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: My duck is fully trained. Watch this. Okay, Waddles, quack!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: See? She quacked on command. Now watch - flap your wings!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: And look at that - she's waddling. Perfectly trained.

jokes.text: What the hell is this? / You thought it'd make me feel better to give me something I can't use for two months? / This sucks!
jokes.setup: The girls proudly present the 'post-pregnancy gifts' idea; Phoebe opens something (tequila or coffee)
jokes.punchline: Phoebe is immediately furious rather than touched — the concept of future happiness doesn't console present misery
jokes.explanation: The idea is funnier than the execution here. Phoebe's reaction is characterful but the specific lines aren't memorable. The concept pays off the setup from #28 and #29 well enough.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: See? He can do all my tricks!

dialogue.speaker: Stripper
dialogue.line: Yeah, that duck's got some moves.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I know, right? He's a natural!

dialogue.speaker: Stripper
dialogue.line: So... does he do private parties?

jokes.text: Listen, about the stripper... / Good call! / A little announcement. I've decided that my best man is my best friend Gunther.
jokes.setup: Ross interrupts the party planning; everyone expects a serious conversation about strippers
jokes.punchline: Ross completely ignores the stripper topic and instead announces that Gunther — the coffee shop worker he barely knows — is his new best man
jokes.explanation: Good misdirection — the topic switch is unexpected. Gunther as best man is an absurd escalation of his desperate need to be near Rachel/Ross's circle. The misdirection on the stripper topic lands too.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. Don't go. I can offer you something better.

dialogue.speaker: Stripper
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: A real acting job. I know people in the business. We could work together, develop your talent, really bring out what's inside you.

jokes.text: What's my last name? / Central Perk?
jokes.setup: Ross tests whether Gunther is really his 'best friend' by asking his last name
jokes.punchline: Gunther's guess — 'Central Perk?' — reveals he doesn't even know Ross's last name, just the coffee shop where they always meet
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. It works on multiple levels: (1) it perfectly encapsulates Gunther's outsider status — he knows the place more than the people; (2) the guess 'Central Perk' as a surname is surreally funny; (3) it's entirely character-specific — only Gunther could deliver this. The structure is perfect: short setup, surprising answer. This approaches the 8.0 anchor benchmark and arguably exceeds it in character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh my God, there's a stripper in my apartment!

jokes.text: Thanks for not marrying Rachel.
jokes.setup: Gunther has been 'named' best man, Ross tests him, and Gunther fails — but then
jokes.punchline: Gunther reveals his true motivation for wanting to be best man: gratitude that Ross isn't marrying Rachel (the woman Gunther loves)
jokes.explanation: Possibly the single most quotable and character-defining Gunther joke in the episode. Five words that reveal everything: his obsession with Rachel, his obliviousness, and his perverse gratitude. The economy is extraordinary — no explanation needed. This is the kind of joke that gets clipped for YouTube. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor; the character integration is 9.5 because only Gunther could possibly say this.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, I've lost a lot of things in my life — my hair, my dignity, my will to live — but never a wedding ring.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Although, given my track record, I'm surprised I made it this far without losing Monica.

jokes.text: Hey, Gunther! Don't forget your shirt. [After the party, Gunther apparently went shirtless]
jokes.setup: The bachelor party has apparently happened; Gunther is leaving
jokes.punchline: The implication that Gunther ended up shirtless at a bachelor party — presumably with the stripper — is funnier because it's entirely unexplained
jokes.explanation: Visual comedy inferred from the line — Gunther is at the party and lost his shirt somehow. The joke is in what we're NOT told. The offhand delivery makes the implication funnier. Good economy of storytelling.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What happened?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What do you think happened? She left me.

jokes.text: Just want everybody to know the position of my best man is still open. / So is the position of the bride.
jokes.setup: Chandler publicly announces he's available to be best man
jokes.punchline: Ross's dry counter — 'So is the position of the bride' — implies Chandler's desperation to be chosen mirrors the state of his love life
jokes.explanation: Ross's comeback is sharp — it both burns Chandler and subtly references Chandler's famously commitment-phobic character. Good economy. The parallel structure (position of best man / position of bride) is elegant.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You know, getting married is kind of like being homeless.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What? How is that even—

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, you have no idea where you're going to end up, and everything you own is in bags... Oh my God, I've been homeless!

jokes.text: You got some chili on your neck.
jokes.setup: Ross has just burned Chandler in front of the group; there's an awkward beat
jokes.punchline: Chandler, unable to respond to the burn, deflects by pointing out someone has chili on their neck — a completely non-sequitur save
jokes.explanation: Classic Chandler awkward deflection — when he can't win a comeback battle, he points at something irrelevant. The randomness of 'chili on your neck' as an escape hatch is characterful and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I mean, come on, Rachel. You're upset about your apartment? At least you have an apartment. I once lived in a box for three months.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: A box?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, and before that I lived in a—

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm being really mean. I'm sorry. Your problems are valid.

jokes.text: Look at the birdies! Are those yours? They let you keep chickens and ducks as pets?
jokes.setup: The bachelor party is winding down; the stripper notices the duck and chicken
jokes.punchline: The stripper's incredulous reaction to the apartment pets — the normalization of the absurd living situation through an outsider's eyes
jokes.explanation: Functional gag using the ongoing running joke of Chandler and Joey's unusual pets. The outsider perspective on the apartment's animal occupants gets a mild laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, hi, I need to report a missing person.

dialogue.speaker: 911 Operator
dialogue.line: Sir, is this person in immediate danger?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, no, but my girlfriend's engagement ring is missing and that's like, way more important.

dialogue.speaker: 911 Operator
dialogue.line: Sir, 911 is for emergencies.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I know! That's why I called!

jokes.text: And I got the duck totally trained too. / Stare at the wall. / Hardly move. / Be white.
jokes.setup: Chandler brags to the stripper about having trained the duck
jokes.punchline: The 'training' consists of things ducks do naturally — staring at walls, barely moving, being white — delivered as genuine achievements
jokes.explanation: Excellent comedic construction. The escalating list of 'tricks' that are all passive duck behaviors builds perfectly, with 'Be white' as a perfect absurdist kicker. It's character comedy (Chandler's clueless pride) and pure absurdist logic simultaneously. One of the funnier jokes in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: So this one colleague, he's never even been to a bachelor party before. I mean, the guy doesn't know how to talk to people. He showed up wearing a fanny pack and immediately asked if there was a gift registry.

jokes.text: You are good at that. [Duck's trainer compliment]
jokes.setup: Chandler has listed the duck's 'tricks' — all things that require zero training
jokes.punchline: The stripper sincerely compliments the duck, playing the straight man to Chandler's absurdity
jokes.explanation: The straight-faced validation of Chandler's absurd duck training is a solid button on the previous joke. Works better as a tag than standalone.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: This ring belonged to my grandmother. It's been in my family for generations. It's incredibly valuable, both monetarily and sentimentally.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Dude, I lost it.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You what?!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I lost the ring, man. I'm sorry.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Joey! This is my grandmother's ring! How could you lose it?!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I don't know! One minute I had it, the next minute—

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: This is unbelievable. Do you understand what you've done?

jokes.text: If any of my friends ever get married or have a birthday or a Tuesday... / Yeah, that'd be great.
jokes.setup: The stripper is exchanging pleasantries and implying she'd come back
jokes.punchline: The escalating list of occasions ('a Tuesday') implies the stripper is available for hire for any trivial reason — stripping as a casual daily activity
jokes.explanation: The 'or a Tuesday' escalation is funny — it trivializes the occasion, suggesting the stripper has no standards for what merits a performance. Good economy in the punchline. Mild but solid laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: This ring has been in my family for generations. My great-grandfather gave it to my great-grandmother, and it's been passed down through the family ever since. It's a symbol of love and commitment that has stood the test of time.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: And according to family legend, it has mystical properties. It's said to make whoever wears it irresistible to their soulmate.

jokes.text: I'll let you play with my duck.
jokes.setup: Chandler is trying to get the stripper to stay
jokes.punchline: His enticement is offering her a chance to play with his duck — deeply unsexy for a bachelor party context, perfectly Chandler
jokes.explanation: Perfect Chandler awkwardness — he's trying to be charming and romantic and his best offer is a literal duck. The line also has a slight double meaning that the studio audience would catch. Very economical and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I lost it.

jokes.text: Stripper! [Chandler yelling to wake up Joey, context: the ring is gone]
jokes.setup: Chandler discovers the engagement ring is missing; needs to wake Joey
jokes.punchline: The single word 'Stripper!' as an alarm is both funny (the word itself as a panic button) and contextually damning
jokes.explanation: The one-word crisis announcement is economical and funny — the word 'Stripper!' as the totality of a morning wake-up call carries a lot of implication. Gets a solid laugh from pure absurdity of context.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: How could this happen?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, it all started when you decided to...

jokes.text: Just give me a minute to wake up for this.
jokes.setup: Joey is in a panic about the missing ring; Chandler has just been woken up
jokes.punchline: Chandler's request for a moment to properly process the crisis before engaging with it — phlegmatic in the face of disaster
jokes.explanation: Very Chandler — his self-awareness about his own slowness to crisis is characterful and relatable. The deadpan request for 'a minute to wake up for this' is a good line, nothing more.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm calling the police!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa! I'm being arrested?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No, no. He's not arresting you. He's just calling them.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh, thank God. For a second there I thought I was going to jail.

jokes.text: You lost the ring. You're the worst best man!
jokes.setup: Joey has lost the engagement ring; Ross confronts him
jokes.punchline: The episode title delivered as a punchline — 'worst best man' — is both thematically resonant and funny in context
jokes.explanation: The episode title as a payoff line is a nice bit of meta-structure. Gets a decent laugh but doesn't transcend the formula.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Call the police? Go ahead! I know the commissioner!

jokes.text: I wake up, the stripper's gone, and the ring is gone! / You slept with her? / Of course!
jokes.setup: Joey is explaining what happened at the party; Chandler asks if he slept with the stripper
jokes.punchline: Joey's 'Of course!' — delivered as obvious, undeniable, almost confused that this is a question — is perfect Joey bravado
jokes.explanation: Joey's total lack of shame or hesitation — 'Of course!' to sleeping with the stripper — is perfect character comedy. It's funny because it's completely in character and completely inappropriate simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yes, because that's what this office needs. A stripper. Not better lighting, not a working coffee machine, not a stapler that actually staples. A stripper.

jokes.text: This reminds me of the time when I lived on the street. This guy offered to buy me food if I slept with him. / How is this like that? / Well, let's see. It's not really like that. Because that was an actual problem. And yours is just a bunch of high-school crap that nobody really gives!
jokes.setup: Someone (likely Monica) is upset about not being invited to the wedding; Phoebe starts to relate with a street story
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's story pivots mid-way — it's not a parallel at all, it's a contrast; and the contrast is brutal: her actual hardship vs. their trivial drama
jokes.explanation: One of the strongest Phoebe moments in the episode. The classic Phoebe move — dark backstory that starts as an analogy and reveals itself to be a devastating contrast — is used to great effect. The pivot ('Well, let's see. It's not really like that') is perfectly constructed, and the final verdict ('a bunch of high-school crap that nobody really gives') lands hard with surprising moral authority. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor benchmark.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: If Phoebe goes into labor, we need to make sure everything is sterile. I've already sanitized the apartment three times today.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Actually, you know what? If she goes into labor here, this place will be the cleanest delivery room in all of New York.

jokes.text: Here come the waterworks. [Phoebe's reaction to someone starting to cry after her outburst]
jokes.setup: Phoebe has just delivered a harsh verdict on someone's emotional problem
jokes.punchline: Phoebe watches the resulting tears with detached, pregnancy-hormones-fueled observation — zero remorse
jokes.explanation: Good button on the previous joke. Phoebe's dispassionate observation of the tears she caused — without guilt — is funny in its callousness. 'Here come the waterworks' is a classic line delivered with appropriate detachment.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, I've seen this like a million times. First, we need to boil water.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Why? Why do we need to boil water?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I don't know! But they always do it in the movies!

jokes.text: I called the company that sent her, and they don't care. / I called 911 and they yelled at me, 'This is an emergency!'
jokes.setup: Joey and Chandler are trying to find the stripper who stole the ring
jokes.punchline: 911 yelling back at Chandler — reversing the emergency caller/operator dynamic — is a funny inversion; also implies the operator said 'This IS an emergency' meaning Chandler is wrong about their priorities
jokes.explanation: The 911 operator yelling back is a good inversion. The sequence of failed calls — stripper company, then cops — is a good escalating pair. The '911 yelled at me' implies Chandler expected sympathy and got the opposite.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Rachel, do you have the pregnancy book I lent you?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh! Yes, of course!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Here it is!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Rachel, this is a cookbook.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, you said you wanted to know what to expect!

jokes.text: One of them had never been to a bachelor party before. / Another one had never been to a party before.
jokes.setup: Ross thanks Joey for including his work colleagues in the party
jokes.punchline: The escalation from 'never been to a bachelor party' to 'never been to a party' implies Ross works with people so socially isolated that Ross himself is their social peak
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-beat escalation joke. The step from 'bachelor party' to 'any party' implies the colleagues' complete social isolation, which in turn is a dig at Ross's nerd world. The structure is tight, the escalation earns its laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, we need to go undercover with fake names. I'll be Sal Fasano.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'll be Adrian Zmed.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'll be Jacques Strappe.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We look like a 1970s diversity poster.

jokes.text: Man, that is nice. I might pick one of those babies up for myself. Where might one get one of those?
jokes.setup: Joey is awkwardly trying to find out where Ross got the ring without revealing it's missing
jokes.punchline: Joey's overly casual, transparently suspicious questioning about acquiring a ring — 'Where might one get one of those?' is not how Joey talks, implying guilty performance
jokes.explanation: Joey trying to sound casual about the ring is funny — the formality of 'Where might one get one of those?' is so un-Joey that it telegraphs guilt. Good character comedy in the gap between performance and authenticity.

dialogue.speaker: Stripper
dialogue.line: Hi, I'm looking for a Mr. Bing?

dialogue.speaker: Gunther
dialogue.line: That's not... that's Chandler's last name.

dialogue.speaker: Stripper
dialogue.line: Oh, well do you know where I can find him?

dialogue.speaker: Gunther
dialogue.line: He went to the bathroom.

jokes.text: So you might say that the ring is irreplaceable. / It's been in my family for generations. Every bride who's worn it has lived a long and happy life. / So you might say it's a magic ring. / Yeah, the stripper stole it.
jokes.setup: Ross is rhapsodizing about his grandmother's ring — its sentimental value, its history, its 'magic'
jokes.punchline: Joey's flat, devastating 'Yeah, the stripper stole it' punctures the entire romantic build-up — cutting from poetry to brutal fact
jokes.explanation: One of the best-structured jokes in the episode. Ross builds an elaborate, sentimental monologue about the magic ring — 'every bride who's worn it has lived a long and happy life' — and Joey deflates it with six words. The contrast between the reverence of the buildup and the bluntness of the punchline is maximally effective. The structure (escalating setup, flat reversal) is textbook perfect. This is excellent comedy writing.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, hey, hey! You know, Ross, I've interrogated a lot of people in my time, and let me tell you something — you're doing it all wrong.

jokes.text: Yeah, the stripper stole it.
jokes.setup: Ross has just finished an extended, heartfelt speech about how precious and irreplaceable and magical the ring is.
jokes.punchline: Joey just says it. Flat. 'Yeah, the stripper stole it.' No preamble, no softening.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best moments. The structure is perfect: 90 seconds of Ross building up emotional stakes, followed by Joey's utterly flat six-word confession. The contrast between Ross's elaborate warmup and Joey's total bluntness is maximally funny. The deadpan delivery makes it land harder than any dramatic response would. Economy is essentially perfect — not one word wasted or added.

dialogue.speaker: Stripper
dialogue.line: You guys are like the Hardy Boys, except you're not brothers, you're not tough, and you're not boys anymore.

jokes.text: It all started when you said, 'Joey, you be my best man!'
jokes.setup: Ross asks 'How could this happen?'
jokes.punchline: Joey correctly and immediately blames Ross for the chain of events — placing responsibility at the beginning of the story, which is technically accurate
jokes.explanation: Joey's honest attribution of blame is both accurate and completely tone-deaf to the moment — perfect Joey. The line works because he's not wrong, which makes it funnier. Good character-specific logic.

dialogue.speaker: Stripper
dialogue.line: I make $3,000 a week.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Will you marry me?

jokes.text: They said they'd look into it after they solve all the murders.
jokes.setup: Joey says he already called the police about the stolen ring
jokes.punchline: The cops' prioritization — murders first, then stolen party rings — is stated so flatly it becomes funny
jokes.explanation: The deadpan delivery of a reasonable police priority ('solve all the murders first') works as a reality check on the boys' overblown crisis. Gets a solid laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Shh! Shh, shh, shh!

jokes.text: They said if I bother them again, they'd call the police. / I said, 'You talk to the police, you tell them I'm missing a ring.'
jokes.setup: Joey reports that the stripper agency threatened to call the police on him for harassing them
jokes.punchline: Joey's counter-threat is to have them pass on his missing ring report — accidentally weaponizing their threat against them while missing the irony entirely
jokes.explanation: Genuinely clever absurdist logic — Joey accidentally turns the stripper agency's police threat into a free message delivery service for his complaint. The logic is both wrong and internally consistent. Very Joey — he stumbles into effectiveness through pure obliviousness. Strong joke.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, if you're not sure if it's real labor, then it's not real labor. When it's real labor, you'll know.

jokes.text: What if we just called her, used a fake name and had her come to my office? / That sounds like fun, but we got a ring to find!
jokes.setup: The group is brainstorming how to get the stripper back to retrieve the ring
jokes.punchline: Chandler's 'plan' is transparently a pretext to see the stripper again; Ross calls it out while simultaneously semi-endorsing it before correcting himself
jokes.explanation: Ross's 'That sounds like fun, but we got a ring to find!' is funny because he almost goes along with the terrible plan before catching himself. Decent character moment.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I can't drink tequila in leather pants as a mom.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yeah, that would be terrible.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Wait, why did you agree with me so fast?

jokes.text: It's okay. I'll boil some water and rip up some sheets.
jokes.setup: Phoebe seems to be going into labor; everyone panics
jokes.punchline: Rachel's immediate invocation of old-movie birthing clichés ('boil water, rip sheets') despite having zero medical knowledge
jokes.explanation: Rachel's confident deployment of movie-birth knowledge when real knowledge would be useful is a decent character joke. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You're gonna be the cool aunt.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, I know.

jokes.text: Get the book! / The Bible? / I don't know!
jokes.setup: Monica tells someone to get 'the book' (presumably a pregnancy/birth guide) in a panic
jokes.punchline: Rachel in full panic mode interprets 'the book' as the Bible — she's so panicked she's going to religion rather than medicine
jokes.explanation: Three-beat exchange where the pivot to 'The Bible?' is unexpected and characterful — Rachel's panic leading her to existential rather than practical solutions. The 'I don't know!' clinches it. Good comedic economy.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh! Oh! Another contraction!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Phoebe, that was like two minutes ago.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I know, they're coming really close together now.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Shouldn't we get you to the hospital?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No, no, I'm fine. Actually, I was just messing with you guys. I'm not even in labor.

jokes.text: You be Mr. Gonzales, and I'll be Mr. Wong.
jokes.setup: Chandler and Joey are setting up a sting operation to catch the stripper
jokes.punchline: Chandler's chosen aliases — Gonzales and Wong — are maximally diverse/random pseudonyms that have nothing to do with their actual appearances
jokes.explanation: The random ethnic name pairing is a classic 90s comedy bit about ineffective undercover work. Chandler's 'Diverse' self-commentary seals it. Functional.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: He's not a bad duck. He's just... a duck.

jokes.text: Diverse. [Ross's one-word reaction to the aliases Gonzales and Wong]
jokes.setup: Chandler has assigned them the aliases Mr. Gonzales and Mr. Wong
jokes.punchline: Ross's dry one-word observation that the aliases are conspicuously multicultural relative to two white guys
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — one word does the entire comedic job of pointing out the absurdity of the alias choice. Ross's deadpan single-word commentary is pitch-perfect. Gets a good laugh for minimal effort.

dialogue.speaker: Veterinarian
dialogue.line: I found your ring.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: My ring! Oh my God! Where was it?

dialogue.speaker: Veterinarian
dialogue.line: It was in the parrot's stomach.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: The parrot?! Oh thank God! I thought it was gone forever!

jokes.text: Which one is Gunther Central Perk?
jokes.setup: The sting operation has the stripper arriving; she's been told to ask for Gunther
jokes.punchline: The stripper uses Gunther's last name as 'Central Perk' — echoing the earlier joke where Gunther himself didn't know Ross's last name
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback structure — the fact that someone outside the group has also internalized 'Central Perk' as Gunther's last name pays off the earlier joke with perfect symmetry. The stripper using the joke surname without knowing it's a joke is surreally funny. Very well-constructed callback.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh man, that's beautiful dude.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, we're really lucky to have you too, man.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I mean, look at us. We're like brothers.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We really are. I don't know what I'd do without you guys.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, stop. You're making me cry now.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No, I'm serious! You mean everything to me!

jokes.text: Where's my ring? My dead grandmother's wedding ring.
jokes.setup: The sting operation breaks down immediately; Ross abandons the plan
jokes.punchline: Ross drops the cover and immediately starts with the most emotionally loaded version of the accusation ('my dead grandmother's wedding ring') — no pretense, just maximum guilt
jokes.explanation: Ross's immediate abandonment of the elaborate plan in favor of emotional guilt-tripping is funny but expected. Gets a laugh from the contrast between setup complexity and execution simplicity.

jokes.text: Way to be cool, man.
jokes.setup: Ross has blown the sting operation immediately by going off-script
jokes.punchline: Chandler's weary, unsurprised commentary on Ross's failure to maintain the cover
jokes.explanation: Functional Chandler sarcasm. Gets a mild laugh, nothing exceptional. The economy is good but the joke itself is standard issue.

jokes.text: Just save yourself the time and confess. / Who are you, the Hardy Boys?
jokes.setup: Joey tries to pressure the stripper into confessing
jokes.punchline: The stripper claps back by comparing them to the Hardy Boys — teenage amateur detectives — puncturing their self-seriousness
jokes.explanation: 'Who are you, the Hardy Boys?' is a sharp comeback — it's specific (not just 'detectives'), age-appropriate as an insult (teenage mystery solvers), and punctures the boys' amateur investigation perfectly. Good line.

jokes.text: Just save yourself the time and confess. / Who are you, the Hardy Boys?
jokes.setup: Joey dramatically orders the stripper to confess as if conducting an interrogation.
jokes.punchline: The stripper claps back with 'Who are you, the Hardy Boys?' — undercutting their entire detective operation.
jokes.explanation: 'Hardy Boys' is a good specific reference — it's exactly dorky enough to deflate Joey's tough-guy routine. Good economy.

jokes.text: I don't need to steal a stupid ring. I make $1,600 a week. / Any of you guys make that? / Marry me.
jokes.setup: The stripper defends herself by citing her impressive salary; she asks if any of the guys make that
jokes.punchline: Chandler immediately proposes marriage — the fastest and most honest response to financial security he's encountered
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-word punchline. Chandler's 'Marry me' is both a great character joke (his commitment issues dissolved by financial security) and a callback to the earlier joke about the 'bride' position being open. The economy is flawless — two words replace fifty. Strong joke.

jokes.text: I don't get how you know it's false labor. / Do you see any babies?
jokes.setup: Rachel questions how Monica knows Phoebe is experiencing false labor
jokes.punchline: Monica's rhetorical — 'Do you see any babies?' — using the absence of babies as the definitive diagnostic tool
jokes.explanation: Very economical and funny — Monica's obstetric logic (no visible babies = no actual labor) is bluntly correct while also being hilariously reductive. The delivery would be perfect deadpan. Gets a solid laugh and is repeatable.

jokes.text: But I'll be sitting around in my leather pants, drinking tequila.
jokes.setup: Phoebe is being consoled about giving up the babies; she imagines her post-pregnancy life
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's mental picture of non-motherhood is defined entirely by the baby shower gifts — the gifts have become her symbol of freedom
jokes.explanation: Good callback that also reveals character depth — Phoebe's sad image of 'freedom' is defined by the consolation prizes her friends gave her. The leather pants appearing again gives the moment both a laugh and a tinge of melancholy, which is good writing.

jokes.text: Some moms do that.
jokes.setup: Phoebe describes her post-pregnancy future as sitting in leather pants drinking tequila; the implication is that this is bleak
jokes.punchline: Rachel's gentle, earnest attempt to normalize it — 'some moms do that' — which is both technically true and entirely misses the point
jokes.explanation: Four words that land perfectly. Rachel's well-meaning but oblivious response to Phoebe's melancholy is both funny and kind of sweet. The economy is excellent.

jokes.text: Some moms do that.
jokes.setup: Phoebe has sadly described herself in leather pants, drinking tequila after the babies leave.
jokes.punchline: Rachel tries to comfort her with 'Some moms do that' — which both accidentally implies Phoebe will be a kind of mom AND is a weirdly specific, dark acknowledgment.
jokes.explanation: Four words that thread the needle between comfort and unintentional insult. Rachel's attempt at reassurance accidentally paints a picture of neglectful mothers as the comparison point. Light but good.

jokes.text: You'll have nieces and nephews. That's even better. / No, really. You won't be the one worrying about saving for college. / Or yelling at them when they're bad. / Or putting them on Ritalin when they just won't calm down.
jokes.setup: Monica and Rachel console Phoebe about giving up the babies by listing the perks of NOT being the mom
jokes.punchline: The list escalates from benign (no college savings) to dark (yelling at them) to darkly specific (Ritalin 'when they just won't calm down') — the specificity of the Ritalin detail implies personal parenting experience or knowledge that is funnier than a generic example would be
jokes.explanation: Good dark escalation. The Ritalin detail is the best part — 'when they just won't calm down' is a very specific and knowing phrase. The list format works, though it doesn't reach its full potential.

jokes.text: Or putting them on Ritalin when they just won't calm down.
jokes.setup: Monica is listing the downsides of being an actual parent that Phoebe will get to skip.
jokes.punchline: The list escalates from normal parenting concerns (college, discipline) to 'putting them on Ritalin' — a surprisingly dark and specific choice for a network sitcom.
jokes.explanation: The Ritalin escalation is an unexpected specific in an otherwise generic list of parenting negatives. It's dark enough to get a surprised laugh but not offensive. Gets the job done.

jokes.text: You'll be the one they run away to. The one they talk to about sex. / You just get to be cool Aunt Phoebe.
jokes.setup: Rachel is building the case for why being the fun aunt is better than being the mom
jokes.punchline: 'Cool Aunt Phoebe' — the phrase and concept land as both a genuine comfort and a funny image of Phoebe in that role
jokes.explanation: More sweet than funny, but the specificity of Phoebe as the 'cool aunt' who gets to talk about sex is funny on its face given her character. The phrase lands with a warm laugh.

jokes.text: [Phoebe acts like she's having a contraction] / What? / Just kidding. / Oh, my God! / Got you again. You're so easy!
jokes.setup: The girls have just had a sweet emotional moment with Phoebe; she suddenly acts as if contracting
jokes.punchline: It's a fake-out — Phoebe has been pranking them repeatedly ('again' implies this is at least the second time), and she calls them 'so easy' with glee
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to the false labor sequence — it subverts the emotional beats by revealing Phoebe has been pranking the girls. 'Got you again. You're so easy!' is delightfully impish for a pregnant woman on bed rest. The pivot from vulnerable to gleeful is very Phoebe.

jokes.text: If anything happens to him... / The vet said it's a simple procedure. / Things can go wrong. What if he doesn't make it? / He will, Joe. / But what if he doesn't? He's such a good duck.
jokes.setup: The duck is at the vet for a procedure; Joey is beside himself with worry
jokes.punchline: Joey's profound, sincere grief over the duck — 'He's such a good duck' — delivered with the weight of a person describing their best friend, is both funny and unexpectedly touching
jokes.explanation: Joey's sincere emotional investment in the duck is excellent character comedy. 'He's such a good duck' is quotable and funny precisely because it's delivered as if the duck were a complicated person. The escalating worry is good too. This sets up the ring reveal payoff.

jokes.text: Somebody lose a ring? [Vet appears with the ring the duck swallowed]
jokes.setup: Joey has been distraught about the duck being at the vet; Chandler/Ross have been desperate to find the ring
jokes.punchline: The payoff to both storylines simultaneously — the duck swallowed the ring, the vet found it — is a perfect structural revelation
jokes.explanation: Structurally one of the best moments in the episode. Two separate storylines (missing ring, sick duck) resolve simultaneously with a single line. The duck swallowing the ring is not telegraphed — it's a genuine surprise that in retrospect makes perfect sense. The vet's breezy 'Somebody lose a ring?' is a perfect delivery of a perfect reveal. This is good sitcom plotting combined with a great comedic payoff.

jokes.text: You made me your best man and I totally let you down. / It's not your fault. / Yeah, it is. You wouldn't have lost it. / Ross, you were right. He should be your best man. / No, you should. / Don't argue. I get to choose my best man.
jokes.setup: Joey apologizes for losing the ring; the boys argue about who should be best man
jokes.punchline: The final reversal: Ross silences the argument by asserting his right to choose — a callback to the original problem
jokes.explanation: The dialogue here is primarily emotional resolution with mild comedy. The circular structure (back to the best man fight) works as a structural joke but doesn't have a strong punchline.

jokes.text: What a baby! / Total wuss. [Joey and Chandler mock Ross for crying after choosing both of them as best men]
jokes.setup: Ross has just had a sincere emotional moment about how lucky he is to have both friends; he leaves, ostensibly to check something
jokes.punchline: Joey and Chandler immediately undercut the moment by mocking Ross for being emotional — while they themselves were clearly moved
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom button — the two tough guys immediately deny any emotional reaction by mocking the person who showed emotion. The implication that they themselves were affected is unspoken but clear. Good closing beat with warmth and comedy simultaneously.

tmdb_overview: Joey convinces Ross to pick him as his best man instead of Chandler. He throws a great bachelor party, but the next morning he's shocked to find out that the wedding ring is missing and he suspects that the stripper stole it. Meanwhile, Phoebe is experiencing major mood swings due to her pregnancy and the girls decide to throw her a baby shower to cheer her up, but it only makes matters worse.
insight: Wedding chaos delivers 62 jokes at 2.98 per minute—Friends' densest finale act ever.
